title: Central-planning tradition
summary: Reframes central planning as a varied family of administrative and computational coordination proposals, separating ownership from allocation and historical command systems from participatory designs.

sources.title: The Socialist System: The Political Economy of Communism
sources.authorityNote: A major institutional account of bureaucratic coordination, direct control, shortage, and soft budget constraints in classical socialist systems.

sources.title: The Political Economy of Stalinism: Evidence from the Soviet Secret Archives
sources.authorityNote: Archive-based study of the creation and operation of the Soviet administrative-command system, including planner-producer conflicts and informal practices.

sources.title: Cybernetic Revolutionaries: Technology and Politics in Allende’s Chile
sources.authorityNote: Archival and interview-based history demonstrating a computational planning project designed around decentralized management and worker participation.

claims.text: Central planning should be classified by dominant coordination and decision rules, not by state ownership alone.
claims.rationale: Ownership identifies who holds formal claims; it does not specify how information, targets, resources, revisions, and enforcement are organized.
limitations: The boundary between dominant administrative allocation and planning within a mixed economy remains a human classification decision.

claims.text: Soviet administrative planning coexisted with managerial discretion, bargaining, concealed information, opportunistic alliances, and secondary exchange outside formal plans.
limitations: Evidence about Soviet operation does not describe every planning proposal or every Soviet period uniformly.

claims.text: Project Cybersyn combined national information infrastructure with a stated design goal of decentralized management and worker participation.
limitations: Cybersyn was incomplete and cannot establish the performance of a mature national planning system.

conflictingEvidence.summary: Kornai and Gregory emphasize systemic pathologies of bureaucratic-command coordination, while Medina documents a planning design explicitly intended to devolve rather than simply concentrate operational control. These accounts concern different institutional forms and should not be forced into one verdict.

limitations: The proposal does not treat the Soviet Union, Chile, socialism, public ownership, or firm-level planning as synonyms for central planning.
The selected cases test institutional variation but do not exhaust market-socialist, participatory, wartime, corporate, or contemporary computational proposals.

relationships.reason: Planning designs specify how dispersed information becomes targets and allocations.
Planning assigns consequential authority and requires explicit contest, revision, and oversight rules.
Administrative systems differ in who may experiment and how errors become visible and correctable.
Formal authority and practical ability to contest planners must be assessed separately.
Information and control mechanisms may change materially with scope, complexity, and time pressure.

proposedRelationships.reason: A bounded historical case of target-led investment, material allocation, forced agricultural transformation, and rapid industrialization.
A bounded, incomplete computational planning experiment with stated decentralizing and participatory aims.
The Soviet case exposes target setting, material allocation, reporting, bargaining, and enforcement as a concrete institutional mechanism.
Cybersyn exposes near-real-time reporting, exception escalation, modeling, and intended worker participation as a distinct mechanism.

duplicateCandidates.reason: This proposal replaces and renames the existing migrated draft rather than creating a second tradition; human review must approve the ID change.

content.description: A varied family of arguments and arrangements that coordinates a substantial scope of production, investment, or distribution through collectively authorized plans and administrative or computational allocation rather than primarily through decentralized market exchange.
content.scope: Classify the institutional dominance and reach of planning, including who sets objectives, supplies information, revises targets, allocates resources, and contests decisions; do not infer the form from ownership alone.
variants: Hierarchical administrative-command planning organized through political authorities, planning agencies, ministries, and enterprises
Indicative and mixed planning that directs selected investment or priorities while retaining substantial market coordination
Democratic, participatory, or computational proposals that distribute modeling and operational decisions while coordinating shared constraints
distinctions: Not synonymous with public ownership, which can coexist with markets or decentralized governance
Not synonymous with socialism, which includes traditions that reject centralized administrative allocation
Not equivalent to planning inside firms, households, militaries, or market economies unless administrative planning dominates the relevant economy-wide scope
Historical command systems and unimplemented computational proposals are different kinds of evidence
commonQuestions: Does central planning mean one office chooses every output? — No; even hierarchical systems distribute tasks across agencies and enterprises, though binding authority and escalation may remain centralized.
Did Soviet plans operate exactly as written? — No; formal targets interacted with bargaining, discretion, strategic reporting, informal procurement, and secondary exchange.

Would better computers settle the planning problem? — No; computation changes processing capacity but does not by itself determine objectives, elicit truthful information, distribute authority, or create contestability.
Is every industrial policy a planned economy? — No; selective public direction and economy-wide administrative dominance should remain distinct.
